goal: Maximize tcp_goodput_bps, the brief's given goal.
limit: The scheduler caps TCP near half of l1 because UDP is locked and still offered 2 Gbps. Queue length 100 and 200 are equivalent; 1000 is slightly lower; TcpBic is 0.03% above TcpCubic, within tolerance, so not better. Other queue disciplines were not simulated, so the recommendation is the best among tested and mechanistically best because scheduler guarantees TCP a service share. Evidence: E1,E2,E3,E4,E5,E6,C5,C6,C7,C8,C9,V5,V6,V7,V8,V9.
explanation: With the default FIFO queue, UDP fills the sender queue and tail-drops TCP; TCP inflight stays at one segment and RTO stalls, so tcp_goodput_bps is 0. Replacing the sender-side FIFO with a per-flow scheduler gives TCP a round-robin service share, about half the 1 Gbps link after packet overhead. Loss-based TCP variants fill that share and deliver about 482 Mbps; Bbr and Vegas underfill it and deliver less. Queue length 100 is enough to keep the scheduler share filled; larger queues do not increase delivered goodput.

claims.text: Default FIFO gives tcp_goodput_bps=0 because UDP saturates the queue and TCP is RTO-stalled.
A sender-side scheduler queue raises tcp_goodput_bps from 0 to about 482 Mbps.
Under the scheduler, loss-based variants TcpCubic, TcpBic, TcpLinuxReno, and TcpNewReno give tcp_goodput_bps within 1% of each other.
Under the scheduler, TcpBbr and TcpVegas give lower tcp_goodput_bps than TcpCubic.
With the scheduler and TcpCubic, l1.queue.length=100 is at least as good as 4, 200, and 1000.
The large spread in tcp_retrans among loss-based scheduler runs reflects different inflight and loss behavior, not higher delivered goodput.
